modules.name: Anatomy & Physiology of Speech, Language & Hearing
modules.desc: The four subsystems of speech (respiration, phonation, resonation, articulation), the brain's speech/language centers and neural pathways, and the anatomy of the hearing mechanism.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The body region located below the diaphragm.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles that move the vocal folds apart (away from midline), opening the glottis.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles that bring the vocal folds together (toward midline), closing the glottis for phonation.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The hard, bumpy ridge directly behind the top front teeth; an articulation landmark.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The nerve-fiber bundle that transmits language information, connecting Wernicke's area to Broca's area.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The fourth subsystem of speech: refining sound by restricting or interrupting the airstream with the articulators. Most associated with shaping consonant sounds.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The movable and fixed structures that shape speech sounds: teeth, tongue, lips, alveolar ridge, hard palate, soft palate (velum), and jaw.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Pyramid-shaped cartilages that sit atop the cricoid. Each has a vocal process and a lateral process; muscles move the lateral processes to bring the vocal folds together or apart.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The nerve that connects to the cochlea and carries hearing messages to the brain.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: If a gas is kept at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional (and have a constant product). Explains inhalation/exhalation: as thoracic volume increases, pressure drops and air rushes in; as volume decreases, pressure rises and air flows out.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A left-hemisphere region responsible for the motor planning and coordination of articulation.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The brain and spinal cord; the pathway along which speech and language messages travel from the brain toward the muscles of speech.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The spiral, snail-shell-shaped structure of the inner ear (within the temporal bone) responsible for hearing.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The 12 pairs of nerves that transmit sensory and motor information; 6 are primarily associated with motor speech.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A ring-shaped cartilage that sits within the thyroid cartilage at its base.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The primary muscle of inhalation, a dome-shaped muscle sitting just below the lungs. When it contracts it flattens, enlarging the thorax; at rest it returns to its dome shape, driving exhalation.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A cartilage attached to the cricoid. It contributes little to speech but plays a major role in protecting the windpipe during swallowing.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The ear canal, running from the pinna to the eardrum.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A special pathway of the central nervous system controlling more gross and unskilled motor movements.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Respiration, Phonation, Resonation, and Articulation — the ordered chain of subsystems that produce speech. All the structures involved are designed for other, more basic biological purposes.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The space between the vocal folds.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The bony front portion of the roof of the mouth.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A bone of the laryngeal region (U-shaped, in the neck) that supports the larynx and tongue musculature.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The middle ossicle, connecting the malleus to the stapes.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Sensory cells in the cochlea arranged by the tone/frequency of the sound they pick up; their stimulation generates the neural signal for hearing.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The raw buzzing sound produced by vocal-fold vibration before it is shaped by resonation into recognizable speech sounds.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The 'voice box.' Its primary function is protecting the trachea and lungs from foreign material; its secondary function is sound production. Built from cartilages — most importantly the thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis, and arytenoids.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The cerebral hemisphere where primary speech and language functions originate for most people.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Passive structures in the thorax that receive air — they do not actively 'suck in' air; airflow results from pressure changes governed by Boyle's Law.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The first ossicle, attached to the eardrum; it is set into motion first, then vibrates the incus.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The cone-shaped bone at the core of the cochlea around which the nerve pathways spiral; it connects to the auditory nerve.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The brain region that sends signals to the speech mechanism to produce the speech that represents the formulated language.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The nose cavity; a resonating chamber, coupled or sealed off from the vocal tract by the velum.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The mouth; a resonating cavity whose shape is changed (by tongue, jaw, and lips) to alter the sound produced.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The chain of three tiny bones in the middle ear — malleus, incus, and stapes — that transmit eardrum vibration to the inner ear.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The oval-shaped opening into which the stapes footplate fits; its motion sets the inner-ear fluids moving.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The cranial and spinal nerves that carry speech and language messages out to the muscles. Includes 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The throat cavity; one of the three resonating cavities that shape the laryngeal tone.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The second subsystem of speech: the production of sound at the larynx. Biological function is airway protection; speech function is generating the raw laryngeal (glottal) tone.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The visible ear on the outside of the head; it helps direct sound into the ear canal.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A special pathway of the central nervous system controlling refined, intricate movements of structures such as the lips and tongue (the articulators).

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The third subsystem of speech: the laryngeal tone is shaped by the size and shape of the pharynx, oral, and nasal cavities. Plays its most important role in shaping vowel sounds (open sounds with free airflow).

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The first subsystem of speech. Biologically it is breathing (O2/CO2 exchange); for speech it provides the 'power' — the airstream that drives sound production. Breathing for life is ~50% inhalation / 50% exhalation; breathing for speech is ~15% inhalation / 85% exhalation (controlled, extended exhalation up to ~15 seconds).

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The inner-ear structures responsible for balance.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The 31 pairs of nerves that, among other roles, are responsible for controlling respiration.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The third ossicle; its footplate fits into the oval window, moving the fluids of the inner ear.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A membrane within the cochlea whose movement (from fluid motion) triggers the inner hair cells.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The chest cavity containing the lungs, diaphragm, and 12 thoracic vertebrae, caged in by 12 pairs of ribs. Changes in its volume drive breathing.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The outer cartilage of the larynx, which may protrude as the 'Adam's apple.' The vocal folds attach to it.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The windpipe; the tube through which exhaled air passes up from the lungs toward the larynx.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The eardrum, located at the end of the ear canal; it absorbs sound energy and vibrates, passing that vibration to the ossicles.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: The soft, muscular back portion of the roof of the mouth. It moves up and back to close the mouth off from the nasal cavity, directing airflow.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: Paired structures of muscle and ligament that attach to the thyroid cartilage and to the arytenoids. Their rapid opening and closing (vibration) in the airstream produces the laryngeal tone.

glossary.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
glossary.def: A left-hemisphere region responsible for language comprehension and formulation.

flashcards.front: What are the four processes (subsystems) of speech, in order?
flashcards.back: Respiration → Phonation → Resonation → Articulation.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Respiration: bio function vs. speech function?
flashcards.back: Bio: breathing / gas exchange. Speech: provides the 'power' (the airstream).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Breathing ratio for life vs. for speech?
flashcards.back: Life ≈ 50% inhalation / 50% exhalation. Speech ≈ 15% inhalation / 85% exhalation (controlled exhalation up to ~15 sec).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: State Boyle's Law.
flashcards.back: At constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional (constant product). Volume up → pressure down → air rushes in; volume down → pressure up → air flows out.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: What is the primary muscle of inhalation, and what happens when it contracts?
flashcards.back: The diaphragm. It flattens from its resting dome shape, enlarging the thorax (volume up, pressure down) so air is forced into the lungs.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Phonation: bio function vs. speech function?
flashcards.back: Bio: airway protection. Speech: produces sound (the laryngeal tone).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Name the four most important laryngeal cartilages.
flashcards.back: Thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis, and arytenoids.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Which cartilage is the 'Adam's apple'?
flashcards.back: The thyroid cartilage (outer cartilage of the larynx).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: What is the glottis?
flashcards.back: The space between the vocal folds.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Adductors vs. abductors of the vocal folds?
flashcards.back: Adductors bring the folds together (close the glottis); abductors move them apart (open the glottis).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: List the 5 steps of the phonation cycle.
flashcards.back: 1) Adduction of the vocal folds. 2) Exhaled air pressure builds beneath the adducted folds. 3) Pressure blows the folds apart, releasing a puff of air. 4) Sub-fold pressure drops. 5) Reduced pressure + fold elasticity snaps them back together — cycle repeats.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: How many phonation cycles per second in males vs. females?
flashcards.back: Males: ~120–145 per second. Females: ~200–260 per second.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Resonation: which cavities shape the tone, and what does it shape most?
flashcards.back: Pharynx, oral, and nasal cavities. Shapes vowel sounds most importantly.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Articulation is most associated with shaping which speech sounds?
flashcards.back: Consonant sounds.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Name the articulators.
flashcards.back: Teeth, tongue, lips, alveolar ridge, hard palate, soft palate (velum), and jaw.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Where is the alveolar ridge?
flashcards.back: The hard, bumpy ridge directly behind the top front teeth.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Broca's area vs. Wernicke's area?
flashcards.back: Broca's = motor planning/coordination of articulation. Wernicke's = language comprehension and formulation.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: What does the arcuate fasciculus do?
flashcards.back: Transmits language information, connecting Wernicke's area to Broca's area.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Pyramidal vs. extrapyramidal system?
flashcards.back: Pyramidal controls refined, intricate movements (lips, tongue / articulators). Extrapyramidal controls gross, unskilled motor movements.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: How many pairs of cranial nerves and spinal nerves? Roles?
flashcards.back: 12 pairs of cranial nerves (6 primarily for motor speech) and 31 pairs of spinal nerves (control respiration).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: What are the three parts of the ear?
flashcards.back: Outer, middle, and inner ear.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Name the three ossicles in order from eardrum inward.
flashcards.back: Malleus (hammer) → incus (anvil) → stapes (stirrup).
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Which structure fits into the oval window, and what does that cause?
flashcards.back: The stapes footplate; it moves the fluids of the inner ear.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Inner ear: which structure handles hearing vs. balance?
flashcards.back: Cochlea = hearing. Semicircular canals = balance.
flashcards.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

flashcards.front: Trace the hearing pathway from eardrum to brain.
flashcards.back: Tympanic membrane → ossicles (malleus→incus→stapes) → oval window → cochlear fluids → tectorial membrane → inner hair cells → auditory nerve → brain.

questions.text: Explain how Boyle's Law drives one full cycle of respiration (inhalation and exhalation).
questions.answer: As the diaphragm contracts and flattens (and the ribs swing up and out), the volume of the thorax increases, which decreases pressure; to equalize with outside pressure, air is forced into the lungs (inhalation). When the muscles relax, the diaphragm returns to its dome shape and the ribs lower, decreasing thoracic volume and increasing pressure, so air flows out of the lungs (exhalation). One inhalation + exhalation completes a cycle.
questions.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

questions.text: List the 5 steps of the phonation process.
questions.answer: 1) The adductors bring the vocal folds together, restricting airflow. 2) Exhaled air pressure builds beneath the adducted folds. 3) Pressure blows the folds apart, releasing a puff of air into the trachea. 4) After release, the pressure drops. 5) The pressure drop plus fold elasticity snaps the folds back together, and the cycle repeats.
questions.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

questions.text: Describe the path of sound through the ear from the pinna to the auditory nerve.
questions.answer: The pinna directs sound into the external auditory meatus (ear canal) to the tympanic membrane (eardrum), which vibrates. That vibration passes along the ossicles — malleus, then incus, then stapes. The stapes footplate moves the oval window, setting the cochlear fluids in motion; this moves the tectorial membrane, which triggers the inner hair cells (arranged by frequency). The auditory nerve then carries the signal to the brain.
questions.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: The Ear (Hearing Mechanism)
notes.body:
The ear has 3 parts: outer, middle, and inner.

OUTER EAR
- Pinna: the visible outer ear; directs sound into the ear canal.
- External auditory meatus: the ear canal.
- Tympanic membrane (eardrum): at the end of the ear canal; absorbs sound energy and vibrates.

MIDDLE EAR
- The eardrum is attached to a chain of tiny bones — the OSSICLES.
- Ossicles (3 bones): malleus (hammer) → incus (anvil) → stapes (stirrup).
- Sequence: eardrum vibrates the malleus → incus → stapes.
- The stapes is the 'footplate' and fits into the OVAL WINDOW, moving the fluids of the inner ear.

INNER EAR — two primary functions: hearing and balance
- Balance: the semicircular canals.
- Hearing: the cochlea (inside the temporal bone), spiral-shaped like a snail shell.
  - Nerve pathways spiral into a cone-shaped bone, the modiolus, which connects to the auditory nerve.
  - Sound/vibration enters the oval window → motion in the inner-ear fluids → movement of the tectorial membrane → triggers the inner hair cells (arranged by tone/frequency) → the auditory nerve carries messages to the brain.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- 3 parts: outer, middle, inner.
- Ossicles IN ORDER: malleus → incus → stapes.
- Stapes → oval window → inner-ear fluid motion.
- Cochlea = hearing; semicircular canals = balance.
- Full pathway: eardrum → ossicles → oval window → cochlear fluid → tectorial membrane → inner hair cells → auditory nerve → brain.
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: The Brain
notes.body:
The brain is divided into right and left hemispheres. Primary speech and language functions originate in the LEFT hemisphere.

KEY AREAS
- Wernicke's area: language comprehension and formulation.
- Arcuate fasciculus: transmits language information (connects Wernicke's area to Broca's area).
- Broca's area: motor planning and coordination of articulation.
- Motor cortex: sends signals to the speech mechanism to produce the speech that represents the formulated language.

NEURAL PATHWAY FOR SPEECH & LANGUAGE
- Central nervous system (CNS): the pathway along which messages travel from the brain to the muscles of speech.
  - Pyramidal system: controls refined, intricate movements (e.g., lips and tongue — the articulators).
  - Extrapyramidal system: controls more gross and unskilled motor movements.
- Peripheral nervous system (PNS): messages pass into the cranial and spinal nerves.
  - 12 pairs of CRANIAL nerves (transmit sensory and motor info); 6 are primarily associated with motor speech.
  - 31 pairs of SPINAL nerves; responsible for controlling respiration.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Left hemisphere dominance for speech/language.
- Wernicke's = comprehension; Broca's = articulation planning; arcuate fasciculus = the connection between them.
- Pyramidal = fine/refined; extrapyramidal = gross/unskilled.
- 12 pairs cranial nerves (6 for motor speech) · 31 pairs spinal nerves (respiration).
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: Resonation & Articulation
notes.body:
RESONATION
Resonation shapes the laryngeal tone by the size and shape of the pharynx, oral (mouth), and nasal cavities.
- Plays its most important role in shaping VOWEL sounds (open sounds with free airflow).
- We change sounds by changing the shape of the pharynx and mouth: opening wider or narrowing, moving the tongue, rounding the lips, etc.
- The velum (soft palate) can close the mouth off from the nasal cavity.

ARTICULATION
Sounds are refined further by articulation; it is hard to fully separate resonation from articulation.
- Most associated with shaping CONSONANT sounds.
- The ARTICULATORS: teeth, tongue, lips, alveolar ridge, hard palate, soft palate (velum), and jaw.
- Tongue moves rapidly to shape sounds.
- Soft palate (velum) moves up and back to close the mouth off from the nasal cavities.
- Alveolar ridge: the hard, bumpy ridge behind the top teeth.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Resonation → vowels; Articulation → consonants.
- Three resonating cavities: pharynx, oral, nasal.
- Be able to list all the articulators.
- Velum/soft palate role: opens/closes the passage to the nasal cavity.
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: Phonation
notes.body:
Phonation is the production of sound at the larynx ('voice box').
- Larynx PRIMARY function: protect the trachea and lungs from foreign material.
- Larynx SECONDARY function: sound production.

KEY CARTILAGES & STRUCTURES
- Thyroid cartilage: outer cartilage; may protrude as the 'Adam's apple'; vocal folds attach here.
- Cricoid cartilage: ring-shaped; sits within the thyroid at its base.
- Epiglottis: attached to the cricoid; minor role in speech but protects the windpipe during swallowing.
- Arytenoid cartilages: pyramid-shaped; sit atop the cricoid; have a vocal process and lateral process; muscles move them to open/close the vocal folds.
- Vocal folds: muscle + ligament; attach to the thyroid and the arytenoids.
- Glottis: the space between the vocal folds.
- Hyoid bone: supports the laryngeal region.
- Intrinsic muscles: ADDUCTORS bring the folds together (close the glottis); ABDUCTORS move them apart (open the glottis).

THE 5-STEP PHONATION PROCESS
1. Adduction of the vocal folds (folds brought together, airflow restricted).
2. Exhaled air pressure builds beneath the adducted folds.
3. Pressure blows the folds apart, releasing a puff of air into the trachea.
4. After the release, sub-fold pressure drops.
5. The pressure drop + fold elasticity snaps the folds back together — the cycle repeats.

Vibration rate: ~120–145 times/second in males; ~200–260 times/second in females.
The result is a glottal/laryngeal tone until it is shaped by resonation.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Larynx: protection FIRST, sound production SECOND.
- Know the 4 key cartilages: thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis, arytenoids.
- Glottis = space between the vocal folds.
- Adductors = together; abductors = apart. (See heads-up note — the lecture handout stated these reversed.)
- Be able to list the 5 steps of phonation and the male/female vibration rates.
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: Respiration
notes.body:
Breathing is both a life function and the first process of speech.
- Breathing for LIFE ≈ 50% inhalation / 50% exhalation.
- Breathing for SPEECH ≈ 15% inhalation / 85% exhalation (controlled exhalation extended up to ~15 seconds for speaking).

KEY ANATOMY
- Thoracic (thorax) cavity: contains the lungs, diaphragm, and 12 thoracic vertebrae; caged in by 12 pairs of ribs.
- Diaphragm: primary muscle of inhalation; sits just under the lungs; dome-shaped at rest.
- Abdomen: located below the diaphragm.
- Lungs: PASSIVE — they receive air; they do not actively suck air in.
- Trachea: the windpipe air travels through.

PHYSIOLOGY — BOYLE'S LAW
"If gas is kept at a constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional to one another and have a constant product."
- Inhalation: diaphragm contracts and flattens; ribs lift and swing up and out → thorax volume INCREASES → pressure DECREASES → air is forced into the lungs to equalize pressure.
- Exhalation: muscles of inhalation relax; diaphragm returns to its dome, ribs lower → thorax volume DECREASES → pressure INCREASES → air flows out of the lungs.
- One inhalation + one exhalation = one full cycle of respiration.

Respiration then feeds into phonation: the exhaled air is forced through points of constriction.

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Life 50/50 vs. speech 15/85 breathing ratios.
- Diaphragm = primary muscle of inhalation; flattens on contraction.
- Lungs are passive; airflow is driven by pressure/volume (Boyle's Law), not by the lungs "pulling."
- Volume ↑ = pressure ↓ (air in); volume ↓ = pressure ↑ (air out).
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing

notes.title: Overview: Speech, Language & the Four Processes
notes.body:
Lecture 1 covers the four subsystems of speech, the brain, and the hearing mechanism.

SPEECH vs. LANGUAGE
- Language is largely innate; speech is learned (innate & learned).
- Key theme: "All of the structures involved in producing speech are designed for other, more basic biological purposes."

THE FOUR PROCESSES OF SPEECH (in order)
1. Respiration
2. Phonation
3. Resonation
4. Articulation

Each subsystem has a BIOLOGICAL function and a SPEECH function:
- Respiration — bio: breathing / O2–CO2 exchange · speech: provides the 'power' (airstream)
- Phonation — bio: airway protection · speech: produces sound
- Resonation — bio: filter/humidify air, eating · speech: shapes the sound from the vocal folds
- Articulation — bio: eating, moving the bolus · speech: restricts the airstream to form speech sounds

★ KEY EXAM POINTS
- Memorize the four processes IN ORDER: Respiration → Phonation → Resonation → Articulation.
- Be able to give both the bio and speech function for each subsystem.
- Speech structures are all "borrowed" from more basic biological systems.
notes.source: Reece Lecture 1: A&P of Speech, Language & Hearing
